Chapter 7. The Power and Limits of Forgiveness.
Forgiveness. It’s a word we hear all the time, but actually living it? That’s a whole different story.
For years, the idea of forgiving his father just felt out of reach—almost like it would betray all the pain he’d been through.
But as the days go by, something starts to shift. The sharp edges of anger begin to dull. You start to realize that holding on to resentment... it’s really just another kind of prison.
There comes this quiet moment—no big confrontation, no dramatic scene—when the son realizes he’s simply tired of carrying all that weight.
And it’s not like flipping a switch. Forgiveness doesn’t arrive in a flash. Instead, it’s more like slowly loosening a knot that’s been tight for years.
Of course, there are setbacks. Old wounds can open back up, especially when a memory surfaces or something new comes to light. Maybe it’s the father’s voice echoing unexpectedly.
But every time, the choice is still there: Do you keep holding on? Or do you try to let go, even just a little?
What’s surprising is that forgiveness isn’t really about the other person at all. It’s about making space for peace within yourself.
But here’s something to pay attention to—boundaries still matter. Forgiving doesn’t mean forgetting, or letting someone hurt you again. You can let go of anger and still protect yourself.
It’s a delicate balance, and honestly, it takes practice. Some days, the pain feels far away. Other days... it’s just as raw as ever.
Having support can make all the difference. Friends, loved ones—they remind you that forgiveness is really a gift you give yourself, not the person who hurt you.
And therapy? It gives you tools—for handling the anger and grief, for sitting with complicated emotions and making sense of them.
Forgiveness isn’t a straight line. It’s a journey, with its own power and its limits. But every step you take toward letting go, even if it’s just a small one, brings a bit more freedom—and a bit more peace.
